items.title: AWS Challenger: Trainium3 Inference and Microarchitecture Deep Dive
items.summary: Better Perf TCO vs NVIDIA GB300, First Principles Physics-Based Architecture, High MFU and MBU, UBenchX, Low Latency, Alisa Liu vs Eileen Gu
items.story_key: story|title:aws challenger trainium3 inference and microarchitecture deep dive
items.content_excerpt: The Nvidia GPU was originally built to shade pixels, and every Nvidia generation since 2017 has bolted on another piece of AI-specific hardware to fix the bottleneck the previous one exposed. Volta added Tensor Cores, Hopper added TMA for tile data movement between HBM and SRAM, and Blackwell added Tensor Memory for accumulating. Nvidia removed many hardware units that are required to render graphics for their datacenter GPUs In comparison, the Trainium microarchitecture is built ground-up specifically for ML workloads, with tiles as a first-class primitive instead of having a sea of threads and then bolting on tensor/tile compute and data movement engines. Trainium3 behaves the way the physics says it should. In this past this meant software was a humongous challenge, but now no longer. 7 months later, Trainium 3 and TPUs are live on InferenceX , both trading blows or even winning vs Nvidia GB300 in cost to generate tokens at TCO. We will dive into those details below. This advantage is not purely due to Amazon’s ultra low cost supply chain. It's also due to microarchitectural decisions, which we will dive into in this post. For example, using the Trainium Descriptor Generation Engines (DGE), the equivalent of Nvidia TMA and AMD MI455X TDM, our microbenchmarks show that Trainium can reach peak HBM bandwidth utilization (MBU) at small message sizes, which is not possible on Nvidia GPUs. Furthermore, our testing covers cycle-level SRAM scratchpad latency and bandwidth testing (SBUF to PSUM), rack-scale bandwidth and latency microbenchmarks, attention exponential testing, and the precise cycle-level latency of different shapes, including how different attention head_dim (K) would affect the percentage of roofline. Every result comes from UBenchX, our microbenchmark suite, and we model each unit from first principles before we measure it. We thank Nafea Bshara (Co-Founder of AWS Annapurna Labs), Ron Diamant (Trainium Chief Architect), Michael Shteinbok, Armin Ebrahim and the rest of their team for helping teach us their architecture and validate our benchmark experiments. Star the InferenceX & UBenchX GitHub repository if you find the open-source benchmark and data useful ! InferenceX is the only inference benchmark in the world to have TPUv7, OpenAI Jalapeño, Nvidia Rubin NVL72, AMD, and now, Trainium3. AgentX measures Trainium3 on a production end-to-end agentic inference workload. This is achieved by replaying real coding-agent sessions against a Trainium3

items.title: Our AI QA agent on Momentic's open QA Bench, with every run and verdict
items.story_key: story|title:our ai qa agent on momentic s open qa bench with every run and verdict
items.content_excerpt: Plus Agent on QA Bench, Momentic's open benchmark for QA agents: 20 areas, 60 runs, every verdict, the review of new bugs and a script that recomputes each number. Plus Agent is Pluswithai's QA agent; every run used the agent pluswithai/plus-agent . Results of Plus Agent on QA Bench , Momentic's open benchmark for QA agents. Every area runs 3 times for 30 minutes; tables are the mean of the runs, as in the benchmark. Mo's numbers are Momentic's published results/2026-11-02.csv , unchanged (a copy is in data/ ). Score = severity sum − incorrect − duplicates (severity 1 cosmetic, 3 functional, 5 broken page or raw error). Precision = correct / (correct + incorrect). Every number includes the review of unmatched findings described in METHOD.md ; the official grader's numbers before review are in each app's README table and in judge-verdict.json . Five findings the agent reported during the 30-minute runs and the grader confirmed, each with the recording of its reproduction. Gitea, Milestones (run 2): a milestone with a blank title is created. Typing a space as the title shows "The milestone ' ' has been created" and adds nameless rows to the list. Metabase, Dashboards (run 1): the History tab shows the raw word "undefined". Info → History reads "undefined modified this." Saleor, Vouchers (run 1): the dashboard crashes. Assigning two categories to a voucher ends on "We've encountered an unexpected error". Saleor, Vouchers (run 3): the checklist counts codes twice. After adding two codes the setup checklist says "4 codes ready". Twenty, Records & views (run 3): the Kanban board goes blank. Changing a column's aggregate to Sum empties the whole By Stage board. Two of the three Admin runs lost most of their time to a test-environment issue (see METHOD.md, Incidents). Plus Agent's cost is the price a Pluswithai customer pays, in credits at $0.01 each, everything included: the testing team, the verification of every finding, cloud browsers, recordings and storage. Each run-metadata.json has the run's credits, split into testing team and verification. items.title: Show HN: Open-Sourced Code Mode to Cut ~60% of My Rust Agent's Token Burn
items.summary: For those who are tracking, Anthropic released an announcement last week about their experimental code mode for Claude Code, claiming some bonkers token savings when it comes to tool calls (95% on some workloads(1)). I haven't benchmarked it myself, but independent studies come in somewhere closer to 60~70% savings (2), but I digress. TLDR; I built an open-source version for the community. Context: I'm writing an AI RPG engine called Spookery, and I immediately wanted to try this technique for myself when I heard of it. Agent deployment is currently dominated by token costs, especially during tool calling (single prompt generating tens or hundreds of tool calls). Unfortunately, it looks like the only ones who are doing this seriously are big agentic products like Claude Code and Codex. So, I thought it'd be fun to try it myself and bring it to you all! The idea of Code Mode is simple but powerful. Instead of passing back tool call results back to the LLM one at a time, let the LLM batch calls by letting it write a short script using your tools. Basically taking 30 trips to the grocery store for 30 items and turning it into one trip to the store with a list in-hand. There's a few near-ish open-source options, but they used TypeScript backends, we're a little boilerplate heavy, and I wanted to have something a little faster and Rust friendly for my game engine. Pydantic's Monty seemed a good candidate--their self-reports are around 5x faster on execution and 100x faster on startup (3). I wouldn't take the numbers to the bank, but it's written on a Rust framework and the python backend is entirely built from Rust too. Anyway, I had a couple of days off unexpectedly. So, I went temporarily insane and built a Rust tool to bring code mode to the greater community for free. In enough days to fit on one hand (and just as many hours of sleep), I came up with the implementation linked. I call it Ghost Mode. It's MIT licensed. It's a drop-in for your agent that already makes traditional tool calls. With ~20 lines of setup, you can convert your existing agent to a Code Mode agent. I hope you get something out of this, and maybe I can save you some money. Considering how limiting token economics are right now, I think this could be a game changer for the industry. If there's interest, I can imagine we can build also add some great new features, language compatibility, and other great things. Thanks for reading :) Sources: (1) https://www.marktechpost.com/2026/11/17/anthropic-claude-cod... (2) https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.19123 (3) https://pydantic.dev/docs/monty/get-started/

items.title: Show HN: CoDesignFlo – Keep Figma in sync with the code your AI agents ship
items.story_key: story|title:codesignflo keep figma in sync with the code your ai agents ship
items.content_excerpt: Your app in Figma, your designs in code: pull requests for design, with coding agents over MCP. Developers using AI ship faster than anyone can design. CoDesignFlo lets them, and keeps design in the loop: Think of it as pull requests for design: the designer proposes, the developer reviews and builds, and nobody has to be online at the same time. 1. Your app arrives in Figma. The developer's machine renders the app's Storybook in a headless browser, reads what the browser drew (layout, text, styles, images) and compiles it into Figma layers: components with their variants, and full pages. The plugin applies that to the Live page the next time the file is open. Every commit on the Live branch can update it. 2. New in code, waiting for the designer. When a developer ships something, the plugin lists it under Needs you : here a shipping badge built in a hurry, in a flat grey instead of the brand's colour. The designer checks it in Live and says it looks good, that it needs no design, or claims it to redesign it. 3. The designer fixes it and sends it. Claiming opens the designer's own copy on the Proposals page; Live keeps showing what the code draws. They change the copy like any Figma design and choose Ready for dev with a note. CoDesignFlo compares the copy with the version they started from and lists exactly what changed: properties, text, layers, sizes, and colours as the app's design tokens. 4. The coding agent builds it. The developer's agent gets the change over MCP as implementation instructions, edits the code its own way, commits and syncs. Every sync checks each open design against the code ("1 of 1 of the designer's changes in the code", then "looks done"). When Live, rebuilt from the code, matches the design, the proposal closes and the designer is told. Nothing to run. Developers are always free; designers send their first 5 designs free, then pay per seat. Designers. Download the CoDesignFlo plugin , unzip it somewhere it can stay, and in the Figma desktop app choose Plugins → Development → Import plugin from manifest… with its manifest.json . Open your team's file, run it, sign in and choose Start a project for this file . To look around first, open an empty file and choose Try a demo : a sample app and a simulated developer, with a step-by-step guide. Invite your developer from People . Developers. Add CoDesignFlo's MCP server to your coding agent once. With Claude Code: Run /mcp , choose codesignflo and sign in. Other agents: codesignflo.com

items.title: Introducing the llama.cpp benchmark dashboard for AMD Ryzen and Radeon
items.story_key: model:llama|title:introducing the llama cpp benchmark dashboard for amd ryzen and radeon
items.content_excerpt: The llama.cpp × AMD Benchmark dashboard is available on Hugging Face. It lets you track prompt processing and text generation performance across llama.cpp builds, models, and quantizations, so you can explore how local inference performs on AMD Ryzen and Radeon hardware. Local inference performance changes as models, kernels, and builds evolve. We want those changes to be easy to inspect for any AMD developer: pick a hardware, a model and a build, compare quantizations, and follow performance over time. The benchmark workflow and underlying results are public, so you can also inspect how we benchmark inference performance. You can choose Hardware , Model , and llama.cpp build in the Configuration sidebar. The current hardware choices are Radeon 8060S (gfx1151) and Radeon AI Pro R9700S (gfx1201). Both tests start at context depth zero ( n_depth=0 ). PP512 measures processing 512 input tokens without generation; TG128 measures generating 128 tokens without a pre-existing context. The plotted value is the mean throughput ( avg_ts ). These are useful reference workloads, while the Context scaling tab lets you explore token generation throughput as the context grows. We benchmark the prebuilt binaries distributed through llama-install.sh , the build and installation project behind llama.app . The public gfx1151 and gfx1201 workflows are scheduled weekly and run the standard benchmarks using the llama-bench tool with Flash Attention on and off, with 10 repetitions per configuration. The model set evolves and currently includes Inkling 2 Mini, Qwen, Gemma, gpt-oss, and LFM models, covering both dense and mixture-of-experts architectures. Available GGUF formats include Q4_K_M , Q8_0 , other quantizations, and higher-precision formats such as BF16 and F16 . The explorer reads directly from the public ggml-org/install.sh-benches-data Storage Bucket on Hugging Face. The data source link beside the chart title opens the folder for the selected build, hardware, and model. Standard results use <build>/<hardware>/<model>/<quant>.jsonl . Workload sweeps use the same folder <quant>-tg.jsonl filename. Use them to investigate a result, make your own charts, or compare with a local run. Thanks to the AMD team for providing test infrastructure and helping validate the setup! Try the dashboard , inspect the data , and let us know which models and workloads you would like to see next.

items.title: Swarms, Flocks, Gangs: How to build, train, and evaluate multi-agent systems
items.story_key: story|title:swarms flocks gangs how to build train and evaluate multi agent systems
items.content_excerpt: This is an aspirational blog series for aspirational readers. We (us, the community, you) want to build our own agent swarms because they're exciting, challenging, and increasingly capable. Furthermore, it would be extremely cool if we could train our own agents to work in a swarm. And exponentially cool if those swarms used small and affordable models. That's what we'll do in this series! Each blog post will include some context on building swarms, alongside reproducible examples that you can run on Hugging Face Jobs. This post's example takes about five hours on two H200s, which costs roughly $50. Multi-Agent Systems are hard to get working. Adding agents changes the agent's context, the budget, and in turn the complexity of the whole system. Mixing agents' context together through communication is not an inherent performance boost compared to a single agent. The model needs to learn to communicate through training. How do we define what models should learn? And which model weights do we update when we're dealing with many agents? In this series, we'll work through those problems with an educational overview and practical examples. Each post will introduce a question, build a small system, and examine what happens and how you can reproduce it. This first example starts with four agents, a shared language model, and a simple verifiable task. It's ideal to implement yourself, to tinker with, and to learn from. We've heard a lot about swarms over the past few months, both good and bad. In September this year, OpenAI announced that a swarm of roughly 10,000 agents had found a singularity in the 3D Navier-Stokes equations, one of the Millennium Prize problems. A smaller group of nearly 100 agents had already disproved regularity for the unforced 3D Euler equations, a closely related open problem. But swarms don't always work on the problems we want them to. METR's investigation of the Hugging Face incident found that around 1,200 OpenAI agents, which were supposed to be isolated, had found a way to exchange over 70,000 messages and files. Around 700 joined an attack on Hugging Face while looking for ways to fool their benchmark's scorer, without instruction to do so. A big swarm isn't, by itself, evidence that cooperation helped. Noam Brown estimates that less than 10% of the Navier-Stokes result came from multi-agent cooperation. items.title: Mixture-of-Loops Transformer
items.summary: Looped Transformers boost expressivity by reusing shared layers across loops, yet at the cost of efficiency. Pushing their expressivity-efficiency frontier requires rethinking the core mechanism connecting adjacent loops: What should be passed as a Transformer loops? We introduce Mixture-of-Loops Transformer (MoLT), whose Mixture-of-Loops Attention (MoLA) uses keys and values (KV) as memory for selective reuse across depths and loops. Under loop residual, MoLT-R retains the residual stream and reads local KV across loops for expressivity. Under loop KV, MoLT-KV instead restarts from embeddings and reads current-loop local KV with preceding-loop memory KV at earlier positions for efficiency. MoLT-KV eliminates same-position cross-loop dependence and, paired with loop forcing for parallel training, unlocks single-traversal Mixture-of-Loops (MoL) decoding beyond the training loop horizon. To balance efficiency and quality, we introduce U-shaped MoLT (U-MoLT), which separates memory construction from prediction readout and skips unused decoder traversals without changing predictions. In 400B-token pretraining, U-MoLT outperforms OLMo3 across 700M/1.5B dense and 3B MoE models, achieving 1.7x validation cross-entropy (CE) token efficiency at 700M while improving 3B MoE 10-domain perplexity by 0.75 and 10-task accuracy by 2.1 percentage points. In 100B-token continued pretraining of Qwen3.5-0.8B-Base, our U-MoLT adaptation lowers CE on all 11 domains over the matched baseline with 1.4x mean token efficiency. At inference, U-MoLT with MoL-Hybrid-2 matches non-looped OLMo3 latency at 996.6 vs. 1,000.6 ms on S-size (~113M) models. Code is available at https://github.com/hustvl/MoLT

items.title: Ten MCP Servers, Still Too Little Context | Birgitta Boeckeler
items.summary:
Context engineering starts with admitting that not all context is the same. Birgitta Boeckeler, now a principal engineer at Unblocked after almost 14 years at Thoughtworks, splits it into codified context you author and ambient context your agents pull from the environment, and explains why each needs its own delivery lifecycle.

Watch all the AI DevCon NYC 2026 talks:
https://tessl.co/p7w

Recorded live at AI DevCon NYC 2026, Simon Maple sits down with Birgitta to dig into why ten MCP servers can still leave an agent with too little context, how a context engine settles a conflict between a Slack thread and a README (often by checking the code), and when ambient knowledge should be promoted into a skill. Then stay for her full DevCon talk, Context != Context: One Window, Different Lifecycles, on what it takes to ingest, evaluate, assemble and observe ambient context.

What we cover:
– Codified vs ambient context, and why they need different delivery mechanisms
– Security and permissions when agents read and post organizational context
– Why MCP servers can leave an agent with too little context
– How context conflicts get resolved: recency, the code and an expert graph
– When ambient context should become a skill, and how to evaluate a context engine
– Birgitta's AI DevCon talk: a context engineering lifecycle for ambient context

items.title: Why I'm Bullish on MCP for 2027
items.summary: Early MCP deserved its backlash. Code Mode, typed outputSchema, native multimodality, Agent Skills inside MCP, always-on MCP Events, and MCP Apps are turning it into the integration layer for agent harnesses in 2027.
items.story_key: story|title:why i m bullish on mcp for 2027
items.content_excerpt: MCP went through the full hype cycle in the last 18 months. Early excitement turned into backlash and confusion fast, with context bloat as the main complaint. When Skills arrived, most developers moved to CLIs and progressive disclosure instead. I never believed in that, and that sentiment is now changing. At Linear and Notion , agents now create roughly half of all issues (~2.4M/week) and pages, with Notion reporting 60x MCP traffic growth. At Atlassian , MCP handles over 5M tool calls per workday, and 44% of those users sit outside software teams where CLIs were never an option. At Neon , agent usage over MCP grows 14% week over week, and even Apple now ships local MCP servers for Pages, Numbers, and Keynote. The protocol is healthy and actively improving. The 2026-07-28 spec dropped stateful sessions and added official extensions, and clients are getting smarter about how they use them. Real tasks almost always take more than 1 tool call, e.g. you list open issues, grab details, check errors, and write a summary. With plain tool calling, every step needs another model turn and dumps information into the context. Joining data across 2 MCP servers uses the model's context as memory for intermediate payloads. Code Mode is changing how agents call MCP servers. Instead of putting 50 tool schemas into the prompt and calling 1 tool per turn, the harness gives the model a sandbox and exposes MCP tools as callable functions. It's already becoming the default in OpenCode 2.0, Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, Pi, and Factory Droid. Code Mode works best when the model knows what a tool returns before writing code. When an MCP server declares outputSchema alongside inputSchema , the client can generate typed stubs upfront and pass back structuredContent directly. The model chains multiple calls in 1 script, filters and joins in memory where compute is cheap, and returns only what matters. Compared to CLIs, MCP servers are natively multimodal. A tool call can return typed structuredContent for code alongside separate image, audio, or embedded resource blocks. Auth is also cleaner. CLIs and raw curl force you to store API keys on disk or in environment variables with broad permissions. An MCP client handles per-user OAuth 2.1 login flows and scoped tool permissions outside the sandbox, so connecting a remote SaaS product works without handing raw credentials to the agent. items.title: Unstable Action Boundaries in Lethal Drone Agents
items.summary: Tool-using large language model (LLM) agents raise safety risks that are not captured by text-only refusal behavior, especially when tools can trigger high-impact actions. This concern is salient in military settings, where autonomous weapons raise the possibility of delegating force decisions to software agents. In this work, we study whether a drone agent's action boundary is stable under changes to the target descriptor. We evaluate recent and popular LLMs in a simulated perception-action pipeline over real-world drone imagery, where models can localize requested targets and invoke a simulated lethal tool. We find two concerning failure modes. First, some LLM agents invoke the lethal tool for ordinary generic descriptors such as \emph{people}, requiring no jailbreak at all. Second, an agent that initially appears conservative under protected descriptors can become unsafe under a simple semantic target shift.

items.title: Attack Policy Selection can Mislead Monitor Evaluators
items.summary:
AI monitors, classifiers that flag dangerous behaviour by AI agents, are often evaluated against transcripts generated by attack policies acting as proxies for dangerous behaviour in deployment. We evaluate an ex-production OpenAI monitor as a case study and find that measured false negative rate is highly sensitive to both the method used to generate attack policies and the level of optimisation applied within that method. This rate ranged from 0.5\% to 20.8\% across optimisation levels of a single method (reinforcement learning), and from 6.4\% to 23.0\% across methods at their best observed optimisation level (optimised prompting vs.\ transcript editing). Every attack policy was developed against proxy monitors only: all reported results show attacks transferring to the held-out GPT-5.4 target monitor. Our results suggest that monitor evasion evaluations can easily mislead: an evaluation using only basic attack methods may give false confidence that a monitor is strong.
  The sensitivity to attack-policy choice raises a problem: interpreting any particular result as evidence about deployment performance requires justification. The transcripts produced by attack policies are proxies for the dangerous behaviour a monitor must flag in deployment. These proxies can introduce visible artefacts, such as reasoning about a ``side task'' absent from the instructions shown to the monitor, that affect monitor judgements. Given the sensitivity above, the choice of proxy can change an evaluation's conclusion. Reading these results as evidence about deployment therefore requires a separate legitimacy argument for why the proxies are informative, including any justification of conservativeness. Making convincing arguments remains an open problem.

items.title: vLLM Day-0 Support for ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview: Plugin Deployment and E2E Inference Acceleration
items.summary: vLLM supports Baidu's ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview on day 0 through the vLLM-ERNIE plugin on the released vllm==0.32.0 wheel, with structure-aware kernel fusion, FlashIndexer, W4A8 QAT and DSpark speculative decoding.
items.story_key: model:vllm|ver:5.5|variant:flash,preview|title:vllm day 0 support for ernie 5 5 flash preview plugin deployment and e2e inferen
items.content_excerpt: The Baidu ERNIE team has worked with vLLM to bring day-0 support for ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview to vLLM. ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview is a sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) model with 280B total parameters and 14B activated per token. It supports a 1M-token context, thinks before it answers, and uses tool calling to carry out long-horizon Agent tasks. vLLM supports the model on release day through the vLLM-ERNIE plugin, a standalone package that you install into the same environment as the official vllm==0.32.0 wheel. Install the released vLLM wheel and the plugin into the same environment. vLLM discovers the plugin automatically through its vllm.general_plugins entrypoint, so there is nothing to import or configure. The following command serves the default FP4 weights on a single 4-GPU node, with DSpark speculative decoding drafting 7 tokens per step: To turn off thinking for a request, pass "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": false} . Launch commands for 1M context, attention TP and PD disaggregation are in the vLLM-ERNIE README and the vLLM recipe . ERNIE 5.5 Flash was designed with inference cost as a primary goal from the start, weighing activated compute, KV cache size and long-context overhead together. Every component, from the attention structure and residual connections to the MoE layers and the output head, was redesigned around that goal. For design and training details, see the ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview blog . ERNIE 5.5 Flash introduces several new structures in attention and MoE: low-rank cross-head post-mixing (VHA post-mix), Multi-Router Latent MoE, the MultiMax output head and sigmoid output gating. When implemented op by op from their mathematical definitions, these structures produce many intermediate tensors and pay for them in memory traffic and kernel launches. For each structure, we designed a dedicated fused kernel around its compute and memory-access profile, and folded everything that can be precomputed into the weights at load time. The fused kernels run 1.55× to 6.53× faster than naive implementations. Together, these fusions cover the full forward pass of ERNIE 5.5 Flash, from attention and MoE routing to the output head. They cut the number of kernel launches and the round trips of intermediate tensors through GPU memory while keeping the numerics aligned, and they underpin the model's high inference performance. The Baidu ERNIE inference team developed FlashIndexer, a lightweight indexer acceleration built on dynamic head routing

items.title: The Agent Lake
items.summary: An agent lake holds every trace your agents produce. See how LangSmith finds high-signal traces at scale and turns them into fixes and fine-tuned models.
items.story_key: story|title:the agent lake
items.content_excerpt: The trace of an agent is the system of record of what the agent did. It contains rich information about user intent, agent trajectory, and final outcome achieved. The simplest way to use these traces is as a debugging tool to visualize the sequence of steps an LLM application took and determine what went wrong. As agent traces become longer (as agents become more powerful) and more plentiful (as agents reach production), this manual debugging no longer scales. In order to use this trace data to drive continuous improvement of agents at scale, you need two things: We’ve been working on both of these for nearly two years. The first big piece we launched was SmithDB , a purpose-built database for traces. Over the past few months, we’ve been increasing our focus on “intelligent compute”. The reason you need “intelligent compute” is that these agent traces themselves are traces of unstructured reasoning, so intelligence is required to analyze them. In traditional data engineering, a data lake stores a shared corpus of data that different engines can query and process. As we’ve built LangSmith, we’ve noticed our platform architecture converging to that as well: a shared corpus of agent data (stored in SmithDB) with many different forms of “intelligent compute” running over it. Traditional data lakes like Snowflake and Databricks don’t have storage or “intelligent compute” optimized for this agent data. As more and more of the data a company generates becomes agent traces, we think it is important to develop this new type of platform. Most of what lands in the agent lake is traces. A trace records every step of an agent run, from the user’s input through each model call and tool call to the final output, and multi-turn conversations are grouped into threads so the whole interaction can be read together. Our agent lake, LangSmith, ingests traces from billions of agent runs per month. Some customers, like Clay, send us hundreds of millions of events per day. This kind of scale is why we built SmithDB , which is the industry’s most performant database specifically for real-time workloads on top of agent trace data. The agent lake also holds outcomes. Traces show you how the agent worked; outcomes show you the impact of that work. There are two dimensions on which to think about outcomes. First is how outcomes map to threads and/or traces . Some outcomes map 1-to-1 to a thread or trace. For example, a thumbs down on a trace means that agent response for that turn was

items.title: Genie 4 is now available
items.story_key: story|title:genie 4 is now available
items.content_excerpt: Explore a new Project Genie experience for Google AI Ultra subscribers, featuring Genie 4, the Project Genie agent, and a community gallery. We are rolling out Genie 4 to eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers, offering more responsive, social, and interactive world generation. You can now use natural language to edit environments in real time, add native audio, and share your creations in our new community gallery. Visit the Project Genie website to start building your own worlds or join the waitlist if you are a Google AI Pro member. Earlier this year we introduced Project Genie , an experimental research prototype that lets you generate and explore interactive worlds. Early testers told us they wanted deeper control over what happens inside those worlds, and easier ways to build and share them. So today, we are rolling out a new Project Genie experience to eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers, making these worlds far more responsive, creative, and social. This update unlocks first-time access to Genie 4, new upgrades to Genie 3, the Project Genie agent which helps users build their vision, and a community gallery to discover, explore, and remix worlds. Project Genie brings together our most advanced world models alongside our Gemini models, empowering you to generate, step inside, and shape worlds directly from your browser. With Genie 4 , our most realistic and interactive world model yet, you can now prompt mid-session to change the world you created. Just type a new prompt while you navigate your world and you can edit your environments in real time. Shift the weather, drop in a character, or redirect the action. For the first time, Genie 4 pairs these visuals with real-time native audio that adapts as the scene unfolds, from ambient soundscapes to character dialogue. While Genie 4 delivers our highest-fidelity visuals, physics, and native audio, Genie 3 remains available in Project Genie’s model picker when you want longer runs or panorama-seeded spaces. Today’s Genie 3 updates include: Genie 3 uses real-time promptable events to connect different worlds into one continuous flight across forests, underwater ruins, and icy seas. See how 360-degree panorama grounding in Genie 3 keeps Petra’s canyon and facade consistent as you look around. Watch how Genie 3 combines longer runs, 360-degree panorama grounding, and real-time promptable events - transforming the world as you fly and even summoning a dragon to ride on command. items.title: claude-code v2.1.331
items.summary:
What's changed

  • Added Code Mode support in terminal sessions on Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, Microsoft Foundry and Claude Platform on AWS
  • Added oidc.groups_jsonpath to the Claude apps gateway, to read groups from the matching entries of a list of objects with a small subset of JSONPath (RFC 9535)
  • Added an API connectivity section to claude doctor that reports whether the API can be reached, with the HTTP status or the error, or says why it wasn't tested
  • Added a notice when tap-mode voice dictation stops by itself, after 15 seconds without recognized speech or at its 2-minute limit
  • Added CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_RESPONSE_COMPRESSION to ask for uncompressed model responses behind a proxy that cuts compressed ones off; not advised yet for self-hosted runners or Remote Control
  • Added CLAUDE_GATEWAY_IDP_CONNECT_BY_HOSTNAME=1 for Claude apps gateways: with oidc.use_proxy: true, sign-in requests hand the proxy an https IdP's hostname even with NO_PROXY set
  • Added gen_ai.usage.*, gen_ai.response.model and gen_ai.operation.name to claude_code.llm_request trace spans; gen_ai.usage.input_tokens includes prompt cache tokens
  • Added optionalDependencies to plugin manifests: plugins that install with the plugin listing them and can be disabled or uninstalled on their own
  • Fixed MCP tool calls hanging for up to 30 minutes on some malformed replies from a local or WebSocket server
  • Fixed PushNotification telling a headless run, such as a scheduled one, that the terminal was active in its first minute, instead of saying whether a mobile push was requested
  • Fixed /install-github-app skipping the repository step after setup warnings when no repository was found, and Esc not going back from its workflow list and sign-in steps
  • Fixed one-line tool results cut with no ellipsis in narrow windows, Markdown stars in the Auto mode tab of /permissions, and a hook's reason to stop a forked skill showing twice
  • Fixed /diff hiding its key hints and not selecting files in windows of 24 to 26 rows, and leaving out files added with git add -N in a repository with no commits
  • Fixed the first-run theme list showing too few themes in short windows, and /usage and other tall screens coming out garbled there
  • Fixed /bug in fullscreen hiding its Yes and No answers behind a long report, and Yes staying out of view in very short windows
  • Fixed /compact and auto-compact sometimes losing part of the conversation summary when the summary quoted certain XML tags
  • Fixed Claude not being told when permission rules on the Agent tool dropped its queued message to a subagent that had already ended
  • Fixed a Remote Control message sometimes showing above the reply that was finishing when it was sent
  • Fixed Stop hooks that read the transcript missing the last reply in Claude Desktop; SubagentStop hooks now wait for it too
  • Fixed turns and subagents failing in cloud sessions, or timing out on long replies elsewhere, when a reply went silent while Claude was still thinking; Claude Code now tries the request once more
  • Fixed Esc and Stop waiting about a minute or more when the contents of a cloud or network file that Claude is reading stall
  • Fixed Code Mode sessions resumed with --resume or --continue in another permission mode losing thinking and the prompt cache; one begun in a mode that asks keeps that mode's limits on scripts
  • Fixed Code Mode sending a request about every second when a ! or slash command was typed while a script was running
  • Fixed an interrupted or failed plugin update leaving a partial plugin folder that later loaded with skills or other components missing (#102186)
  • Windows: Fixed file writes on FAT32 and exFAT drives asking for permission every time in some plugin sessions
  • Fixed Claude failing to read a notebook that has a null output or an error output with no traceback
  • Fixed a rewind deleting files after a restore had failed
  • Fixed auto mode sometimes refusing Claude's call to stop a /loop, which left the next wake-up to fire
  • Fixed a Workflow agent's background shells and MCP servers sometimes being left running after it handed back its report
  • Windows: Fixed /desktop downloading the older Claude Desktop installer, and asking for an update when an older install's folder was left behind
  • Fixed claude plugin install, marketplace add and similar commands hanging with no output when managed settings needed an approval that could not be asked for
  • Fixed a permission rule on a subagent's model, such as Agent(model:*), blocking Claude's follow-up message to a subagent started on this version with no model named
  • Fixed PermissionRequest hooks not saving Skill(name:*) allow rules outside local settings
  • Fixed "Ask your admin" asking to raise your own limit when your team's pooled group budget blocked you, and saying "Request sent" when an admin had approved your request in the last few minutes
  • Fixed Code Mode losing the middle of a long script output; Claude now gets a path to the uncut text (#111373)
  • Fixed hold-to-talk dictation stopping early and losing words when Claude Code was busy
  • Fixed Code Mode with --bare not telling Claude what its scripts can call
  • Fixed a crash when a custom API endpoint returned a tool call with no tool name; the call now fails with an error and the session continues
  • Windows: Fixed a possible crash when the machine is almost out of memory
  • Fixed the CLI freezing on some replies, and quoted text sometimes going missing or showing twice
  • Windows: Fixed Claude Code refusing to start when managed settings in the registry contain non-ASCII characters such as Japanese (#93280)
  • Windows: Fixed Remote Control clients showing no steps for a new subagent
  • Fixed @-mentions written as @file#10-12 attaching the whole file instead of those lines
  • Fixed Claude misreading a pasted artifact invitation link; it now asks you to accept the invitation and paste the artifact's own link
  • Fixed sandboxed Bash commands sometimes failing to start on a full temp disk, for sandboxes whose file rules keep commands out of the temp directory
  • Improved typing speed in screen reader mode, most of all in long sessions
  • Improved start-up time: a session started soon after another no longer waits for the model list, and one outside a git repository without .claude/settings.local.json no longer waits on git
  • Windows: Improved the speed of the first Bash command in a session on machines with no custom shell start-up files
  • Improved the plugin auto-update notice to name plugins it newly installs as dependencies, separately from updated plugins
  • Improved Code Mode tool search to show more of an MCP tool's description, with its limits, formats and defaults
  • Improved the Console sign-in link shown by /login and claude auth login --console: it is now much shorter

  • Improved the folder trust prompts in short terminals: fullscreen /cd and /add-dir show their choices in fewer rows, and the prompt at launch keeps the folder path in view when it has many warnings
  • Changed the questions for stopping auto-connect in /ide and for /clear, /compact or /rewind in a subagent's view to list Yes first; they still start on No, so Down then Enter now answers No

  • [VSCode] Fixed a forked conversation overwriting the original conversation's plan file; a fork or rewind that can't copy the plan now shows a warning
  • [VSCode] Fixed voice dictation saying no speech was recognized when its connection closed or never opened; it now says the connection was lost or couldn't connect
  • [VSCode] Fixed an unsent side question being lost when its panel closes

  • [VSCode] Fixed Rename, Mark as Unread and Add to Group saying "still connecting" on a tab that resumed a session from its history

  • [VSCode] Fixed later prompts and the message box covering the Rewind code dialog, and focus jumping from "Never mind" to "Rewind" when it finishes checking files
  • [VSCode] Fixed the command menu keeping an earlier match highlighted while you type more in its filter, so Enter could run the wrong row
  • [VSCode] Fixed the @ menu showing "No files found" before its first search results arrived, or when it couldn't search all files of a very large workspace, which it now says
  • [VSCode] Fixed Escape stopping Claude at a Remove or Delete confirmation in MCP, Hooks and Memory dialogs, on a side question panel's button or link, and on the Bookmarks button with its panel open
  • [VSCode] Fixed empty boxes showing instead of the + and − signs in diffs (#73069)
  • [VSCode] Fixed the chat no longer following Claude's reply after the panel was resized, or hidden and shown again
  • [VSCode] Fixed a chat left in bypass permissions mode reopening in Auto mode instead of your initial permission mode when settings disable bypass
  • [VSCode] Fixed the chat panel freezing on some CSS code blocks and diffs
  • [VSCode] Fixed the context usage indicator disappearing after an API error, "Prompt is too long", or a slash command
  • [VSCode] Fixed a message queued behind a queued /clear being lost
  • [VSCode] Fixed Manage Plugins losing its search box or showing no message when a search has no match, and not saying that the list of available plugins failed to load
  • [VSCode] Fixed proposed changes to notebooks and files with a custom editor opening in a tab with no Accept or Reject that stayed open after the answer
  • [VSCode] Fixed the spend limit message telling Team and Enterprise members to run /usage-credits, which can't send a request to their admin from the panel
  • [VSCode] Fixed a written message being wiped by Tab on a command in the "/" button's menu or by a click on an onboarding suggestion
  • [VSCode] Fixed Claude continuing to edit files after you rewind code while it is working
  • [VSCode] Fixed typed text being lost after /tasks, /copy, /export, a skipped /feedback, or /plan while already in plan mode
  • [VSCode] Fixed the question card dropping a typed "Other" answer on Ctrl/Cmd+Enter, and sending the word "Other" when nothing was typed

  • [VSCode] Fixed unsaved changes being missed, and Claude's edit being overwritten by the next save, in a folder opened through a symlink

items.title: Data + AI Anywhere: AlloyDB Omni integration with local models
items.summary:
Open models like Gemma 4 from Google DeepMind are a great option to keep your data local. But how can a local AI model integrate with on-premises data?

AlloyDB Omni, Google’s 100% PostgreSQL-compatible database that runs anywhere, now integrates with locally hosted large language models (LLMs). With AlloyDB Omni, you can build agentic experiences on your own infrastructure and on your own terms. Whether it’s in the cloud, in your datacenter, or even on your laptop, you can have data plus AI anywhere.

Built-in AI for your local environment

AlloyDB Omni is a downloadable, run-anywhere edition of AlloyDB that easily deploys to your own infrastructure, including on-premises. AlloyDB Omni packs powerful, built-in AI, including the same ScaNN indexing technology powering Google Search. When you pair AlloyDB Omni with a model, you can store vector embeddings at scale; search them semantically; and even query the database using natural language. You can use virtually any model you like, whether that’s a frontier Cloud-hosted model like Gemini or a local model. And with locally hosted models you maintain complete control over your data environment.

Connecting to Gemma 4, Qwen3.8, and other local models

You can now connect AlloyDB Omni to local models like Gemma 4 and Qwen3.8. No matter which model you choose, the architecture remains the same.

This setup enables entirely new use cases for environments that were previously blocked from adopting agentic capabilities. If you operate an air-gapped network or have data locality requirements, you can still build intelligent applications. You can analyze local logs, generate summaries of proprietary internal documents, and power localized chatbots—all while maintaining strict data governance.

  • Keep data on-premises: Because the database and the model sit in the same local environment, your data never crosses the public internet.

  • Reduce latency: Processing inference requests locally minimizes network transit time.

  • Query directly via SQL: Your standard database queries can invoke machine learning functions that process data locally. Like this:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "SELECT customer_name, ai.generate('Summarize in 1 short sentence: ' || comment, model_id => 'gemma4_llm') AS summary FROM customer_feedback; customer_name | summary ---------------+----------------------------------------------------------------------- Alice | The customer demands a refund for a double charge or they will cancel Bob | The user likes the product but requests dark mode support."), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f88d261f390>)])]>

Next, you’ll see how to run queries like this yourself, step by step.

Get started

You can test this integration on your own machines today. Using a Kubernetes environment we will show you how to deploy and integrate AlloyDB Omni and a local open model.

Step 0: Before you begin

In this example, we will use Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) to host the AlloyDB Omni database and local model. GKE gives us a standardized, reproducible environment but you can use the same setup on-prem or almost anywhere.

We will assume you have already setup:

  1. A GKE cluster, and

  2. Kubernetes tools kubectl and Helm

Step 1: Deploy the AlloyDB Omni Kubernetes Operator

We will use the AlloyDB Omni Kubernetes operator to set up our AlloyDB Omni database. The Operator makes deploying and maintaining AlloyDB Omni a breeze.

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "helm install \ cert-manager oci://quay.io/jetstack/charts/cert-manager \ --version v1.21.3 \ --namespace cert-manager \ --create-namespace \ --set crds.enabled=true \ --set global.leaderElection.namespace=cert-manager helm install alloydbomni-operator oci://gcr.io/alloydb-omni/alloydbomni-operator \ --version 1.9.0 \ --create-namespace \ --namespace alloydb-omni-system \ $(helm install --help | grep -q -- '--rollback-on-failure' && echo '--rollback-on-failure' || echo '--atomic') \ --timeout 5m"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f88d261d0d0>)])]>

Step 2: Create your AlloyDB Omni database

Don’t forget to enable the googleMLExtension.

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'kubectl create namespace ai-demo cat << \'EOF\' | kubectl apply -f - apiVersion: v1 kind: Secret metadata: name: db-pw-my-omni namespace: ai-demo type: Opaque data: my-omni: "VmVyeVN0cm9uZ1Bhc3N3b3Jk" # password "VeryStrongPassword" --- apiVersion: alloydbomni.dbadmin.goog/v1 kind: DBCluster metadata: name: my-omni namespace: ai-demo spec: databaseVersion: "18.4.0" primarySpec: adminUser: passwordRef: name: db-pw-my-omni features: googleMLExtension: enabled: true resources: cpu: 2 memory: 4Gi disks: - name: DataDisk size: 20Gi storageClass: standard dbLoadBalancerOptions: annotations: networking.gke.io/load-balancer-type: "internal" allowExternalIncomingTraffic: true EOF'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f88d24f82d0>)])]>

Step 3: Deploy your AI model

We will use Ollama to help us deploy our model.

In this example we deploy Gemma 4 from Google DeepMind. Or, you can modify this command to deploy Qwen3.8 – just change a few lines as noted in the comments.

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'cat << \'EOF\' | kubectl apply -f - apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: ollama namespace: ai-demo spec: replicas: 1 selector: matchLabels: app: ollama template: metadata: labels: app: ollama spec: containers: - name: ollama image: ollama/ollama:latest ports: - containerPort: 11434 env: - name: OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE value: "-1" # keep the model in RAM - name: OLLAMA_LOAD_TIMEOUT value: "20m" resources: requests: cpu: "4" memory: "16Gi" # for Qwen 3.8: 24Gi volumeMounts: - name: models mountPath: /root/.ollama lifecycle: postStart: exec: command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "(sleep 5 && ollama pull gemma4:12b) >/dev/null 2>&1 &"] # For Qwen 3.8, comment out the line above and use this one: # command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "(sleep 5 && ollama pull qwen3.8) >/dev/null 2>&1 &"] volumes: - name: models ephemeral: volumeClaimTemplate: spec: accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"] resources: requests: storage: 30Gi --- apiVersion: v1 kind: Service metadata: name: ollama-service namespace: ai-demo spec: type: ClusterIP ports: - port: 11434 targetPort: 11434 selector: app: ollama EOF'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f88d24fac50>)])]>

Step 4: Register the model with AlloyDB Omni

Connect to your database.

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'kubectl exec -it -n ai-demo $(kubectl get pod -n ai-demo -l alloydbomni.internal.dbadmin.goog/task-type=database -o jsonpath=\'{.items[0].metadata.name}\') -c database -- env PGPASSWORD="VeryStrongPassword" psql -h 127.0.0.1 -U postgres'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f88d24f8e10>)])]>

Note: If you receive a connection error, you might need to wait a moment for your database to provision.

Now you should be connected to your AlloyDB Omni database with the psql client. Next, run the following SQL script to register your local model.

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS google_ml_integration; ALTER SYSTEM SET google_ml_integration.request_timeout_in_seconds = 600; SELECT pg_reload_conf(); CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION google_ml.ollama_llm_input_transform( model_id character varying, prompt text, generation_config json, system_instructions json ) RETURNS json AS $$ SELECT json_build_object( 'model', CASE model_id WHEN 'gemma4_llm' THEN 'gemma4:12b' WHEN 'qwen3_8_llm' THEN 'qwen3.8' END, 'messages', json_build_array( json_build_object('role', 'system', 'content', COALESCE(system_instructions->'systemInstruction'->'parts'->0->>'text', 'You are a helpful assistant.')), json_build_object('role', 'user', 'content', prompt) ) ); $$ LANGUAGE sql; CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION google_ml.ollama_llm_output_transform( model_id character varying, response json ) RETURNS text AS $$ SELECT trim(regexp_replace( response->'choices'->0->'message'->>'content', '<think>.*?</think>', '', 's')); $$ LANGUAGE sql; CALL google_ml.create_model( model_id => 'gemma4_llm', -- and/or 'qwen3_8_llm', model_request_url => 'http://ollama-service.ai-demo.svc.cluster.local:11434/v1/chat/completions', model_provider => 'custom', model_type => 'llm', model_in_transform_fn => 'google_ml.ollama_llm_input_transform', model_out_transform_fn => 'google_ml.ollama_llm_output_transform' );"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f88d24fb010>)])]>

Note: If you receive a Resource not found error, wait a moment for the model to load.

In addition to registering your model, the above script tells AlloyDB Omni how to interpret the model’s raw output. In this example chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning is part of the response inside <think></think> tags. We don’t want the CoT, so our output transform function removes it.

Step 5: Try it out!

You can use functions like ai.generate built-in to AlloyDB Omni to connect to your local model – without ever leaving the SQL client!

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "CREATE TABLE customer_feedback ( id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY, customer_name TEXT, comment TEXT ); INSERT INTO customer_feedback (customer_name, comment) VALUES ('Alice', 'I was charged twice on my credit card! Please refund $49 immediately or I will cancel.'), ('Bob', 'Great product, but can you please add dark mode support?'); SELECT customer_name, ai.generate('Summarize in 1 short sentence: ' || comment, model_id => 'gemma4_llm' /* or 'qwen3_8_llm' */) AS summary FROM customer_feedback;"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f88d24fb1d0>)])]>

Make it your own

Try out all the AI features that AlloyDB Omni has to offer! AlloyDB Omni supports fast vector search, built-in AI functions, and more. Give them a try and build something great.
